subject: convergence in Poisson with very large values

messages.author: 2430f2828c808219
messages.subject: convergence in Poisson with very large values
parts:
Hi all

The attached model tries to fit a Poisson distribution to discrete counts that have an expectation of ca. 40,000,000.  I do know that the normal is going to be a very good approximation in these circumstances, but what if we wanted to stick with the Poisson.  Arguably, we should be able to fit it, shouldn't we?  And in fact, the glmer function in the lme4 R package seems to be able to do so.  But, rstan (v2.7) does a really poor job in this parameter space.  I suspect that this is because of the factorial in the Poisson likelihood and any associated overflow could be avoided by incrementing the log probability without the factorial, as it is a constant (but I haven't tried this yet).

The main question I had now was whether stan should be able to fit this model in the first place, especially as glmer seems able to return something sensible?  I've attached self-contained code that compares the two approaches.

Thanks
Andrew

On Monday, September 14, 2015 at 2:14:13 PM UTC-4, atzap wrote:
But, rstan (v2.7) does a really poor job in this parameter space.  I suspect that this is because of the factorial in the Poisson likelihood and any associated overflow could be avoided by incrementing the log probability without the factorial, as it is a constant (but I haven't tried this yet).

The build-in sampling statements in Stan already do that. I think it would be fine if you Matt trick the group means with something like

parameters{
 real intercept;
 real<lower = 0, upper = 100> sigma;
 real groupvar_raw[10];
  }
transformed parameters{
  real mu[1000];
  for (i in 1:1000)
   mu[i] <-  intercept + sigma * groupvar_raw[group[i]];
}
model {
  groupvar_raw ~ normal(0,1);
  y ~ poisson_log(mu);
}

The overly diffuse priors on the intercept and sigma probably aren't helping you, but I can model these simulated data fine locally.

On Monday, September 14, 2015 at 3:53:24 PM UTC-4, atzap wrote:
On Monday, September 14, 2015 at 8:23:01 PM UTC+1, Ben Goodrich wrote:
The build-in sampling statements in Stan already do that. I think it would be fine if you Matt trick the group means with something like

Thanks Ben.  I simplified this example quickly from something much more complicated so could have definitely been more efficient in terms of vectorizing by group (as Bob suggests) or using the Matt trick.

The Matt trick is not primarily about efficiency in the sense of how fast it takes to computer to execute a function; it is about changing the geometry of the posterior distribution so that Stan can sample from the posterior distribution efficiently (in the sense of quickly converging to the posterior distribution, having low dependence among consecutive draws, exploring the tails, etc.).

So I guess I want to ask whether is there any good reason why we can't recover the estimates without the Matt trick, especially if it isn't an issue associated with the dropping the constants (which I had forgotten that Stan does).

In many cases with multilevel models, it is not possible for Stan to sample efficiently without the Matt trick. That isn't a universal rule but in this case, I think it is necessary.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: convergence in Poisson with very large values
parts:
It might sample as written with reasonable initial values, or
with the centered parameterization (fully non Matt tricked version),

group[k] ~ normal(intercept, sigma);

and then you don't need to add the intercept for mu. You might also
get by with tighter priors. But as written with our default inits you're
right it doesn't work.

The problem is that it's not converging in the warmup span given. What
happens with the problem as originally written is that chains get stuck with
the wrong fixed effect with the group-level effects compensating with higher values
and hence a higher std deviation because values are (non-)centered around 0.

The centered parameterization can help here (opposite of the Matt trick),
as can tighter priors, which can tamp down the deviation of the group-level
effects. It's difficult for the sampler to move away from this suboptimal solution
because of the correlation between the hierarchical standard deviation and the
values of the group effects. You need to simultaneously move to lower
standard deviation and smaller group-level effects and higher fixed effect.
It's basically the usual problem in a hierarchical model as illustrated
by the funnel in the manual chapter on problematic posteriors.

It might also work as written with reasonable initial values.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] convergence in Poisson with very large values
parts:
The new model's suffering from identifiability problems in
that it's not mixing across various parameter values. Each chain
gets stuck with slightly different values, and nearly indistinguishable
log densities.

I don't know lme4 well enough to understand what this means:

glmer(y ~ 1 + (1|mont) + (1|year) + (1|seq(1:N)), family = "poisson")

But the Stan model has this

mu[i] <- intercept + sigmaMont*varmont[mont[i]] + sigmaYear*varyear[year[i]] + sigmaERR*inderr[i];

with inderr[i] being a parameter per mu[i] that is only conditioned on y[i]:

y[i] ~ poisson_log(mu[i])

But that doesn't seem to be giving you enough information to really fit
it well.

Won't inderr[i] * sigmaERR just drift to y[i] - the other terms in mu[i] or
thereabouts? Are you using sigmaERR in an effort to estimate the error in
mu[i] without the inderr terms? I'd think you could just do that as a residual
analysis. But even removing sigmaERR doesn't help with it fitting.

You also have the additive non identifiability of intercept,
sigmaYear * varyear, and sigmaMont * varmont, which the priors don't seem
to be strong enough to identify.

I'm not sure how lme4 can sort this out.

Andrew's going to tell you not to use those interval priors, but more
Andrew-friendly priors also don't work here, so I don't have any suggestion
for fixing this model.

- Bob

P.S. for everyone else, here's the model

data{
int<lower = 0> N;
int<lower = 0> Nyrs;
int<lower = 0> Nmth;
int y[N];
int<lower=0> mont[N];
int<lower=0> year[N];
}
parameters{
real intercept;
real<lower = 0, upper = 10> sigmaERR;
real<lower = 0, upper = 10> sigmaYear;
real<lower = 0, upper = 10> sigmaMont;
real inderr[N];
real varyear[Nyrs];
real varmont[Nmth];
}
transformed parameters{
real mu[N];
for (i in 1:N)
mu[i] <- intercept + sigmaMont*varmont[mont[i]] + sigmaYear*varyear[year[i]] + sigmaERR*inderr[i];
}
model{
intercept ~ normal(17, 1);
varmont ~ normal(0, 1);
varyear ~ normal(0, 1);
inderr ~ normal(0, 1);
y ~ poisson_log(mu);

}

Hi Bob

What makes you think that the chains are getting stuck and it is not something else?  I've tried jittering the stepsize and that doesn't seem to help.

The model that I am trying to fit has an observation-level random effect.  That is what you are seeing in the glmer code.  And this is often referred to as a Poisson-lognormal distribution.  Here is a widely-cited paper on it:  http://www.abdn.ac.uk/lambin-group/Papers/Paper%2041%202001%20Elston%20Tick%20aggregation%20Parasitology.pdf.  The observation-level effect essentially soaks up the residual error left over from the other terms and is useful for dealing with over-dispersion.

I have fitted this type of model many times in Stan without any issue.  It seems that this particular problem is confined to the large values of y.  If you divide y by 400,000 and round to integers, for example, the model fits fine in Stan (though remember to relax the informative prior on the intercept).  The estimates also match glmer.  Again, to me this flags up an issue with large integer values and Stan's Poisson calculations/sampling.

Thanks
Andrew

parts:

It's very clear from the traceplots. Each chain settles into
a region of parameter space with different values. That's all I mean
by "stuck" --- they're stuck around their own modes. You can also see
that the modes are relatively close together in log density.

> The model that I am trying to fit has an observation-level random effect. That is what you are seeing in the glmer code. And this is often referred to as a Poisson-lognormal distribution. Here is a widely-cited paper on it: http://www.abdn.ac.uk/lambin-group/Papers/Paper%2041%202001%20Elston%20Tick%20aggregation%20Parasitology.pdf. The observation-level effect essentially soaks up the residual error left over from the other terms and is useful for dealing with over-dispersion.

I see the soaking effect in the model but will have to look
at the paper to see why this is useful --- I can see the analogy
to the more familiar (to me) negative binomial (gamma-Poisson).

> I have fitted this type of model many times in Stan without any issue. It seems that this particular problem is confined to the large values of y. If you divide y by 400,000 and round to integers, for example, the model fits fine in Stan (though remember to relax the informative prior on the intercept). The estimates also match glmer. Again, to me this flags up an issue with large integer values and Stan's Poisson calculations/sampling.

Clearly that points to large values, but it's likely to be more about
scaling and adaptation than instability of the Poisson calculation. On
the log scale with log scale parameter, it's just

log pois_log(y | alpha) = k * alpha - log y! - exp(alpha)

The exp() might be problematic here given that alpha is around 17 or so.
It means small moves in alpha are quite large moves in exp(alpha).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: non-convergence with Poisson with lambda approx exp(17) approx 25M
parts:
This definitely won't converge. I'm attaching a standalone Stan model
and R dump formatted data so Michael might be able to take a look at it.
The basic idea is that there's an item-level lognormal random effect
contributing to the mean parameter for the Poisson --- it's an alternative
to the gamma you find in the negative binomial for overdispersion that
makes the whole thing compatible with being run as a GLM.

The basic behavior really jumps around with the epochs of fast/slow
adaptation, so I think they may be overtuning in some sense. It then
always drifts during sampling --- that is, even 20K warmup iterations starting
from small initial step size (0.001) and high acceptance target (0.99) doesn't
get to where it should.

I'm not sure what's going on. But it's definitely not converging. I
tried much tighter priors, not using intervals on sd, +/- Matt trick, etc.
I tried very small step sizes, very large tree depth, etc. Some just
ground to a halt so I didn't have patience to go on.

I wonder if it could be something as basic as scale required for regularization
in our mass matrix estimation.

lme4 recovers the parameters no problem (and almost instantly, to boot).

What appears to happen is that each chain gets stuck in its own local
part of the parameter space --- that is, it only seems to be weakly
identified.

With much smaller sizes, the OP (atzap) said it converges. I haven't
tried.

Of course, in this case, a normal approximation is probably warranted, so
I'm not too worried about this particular model --- it's just that I want
to understand what's going on with the sampler.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: non-convergence with Poisson with lambda approx exp(17) approx 25M
parts:
It's probably something to do with scaling step sizes or the
mass matrix or the curvature when you get into that zone of
the Poisson. I don't think it's an arithmetic instability of
the usual kind (overflow, underflow, loss of precision, etc.) or
a bug in the sampler. Instead, I think this is something we're
either not going to be able to fit with Euclidean HMC or something
where we'll have to do a better job of adaptation.

Thanks for bringing it to our attention.

- Bob

One thing to consider is convergence — using our standard inits the parameter “intercept”
will be off by its prior equilibrium value (initialized to ~0 when it needs to get to ~17). This
long convergence (and the large gradients out in that tail) could be skewing the adaptation.
Try writing something like

...

transformed parameters{
real mu[N];
for (i in 1:N)

mu[i] <- 17 + intercept + sigmaMont*varmont[mont[i]] + sigmaYear*varyear[year[i]] + sigmaERR*inderr[i];
}
model{
intercept ~ normal(0, 1);
…

and see if that’s any better.

Alternatively, just turn adaptation off and see how the sampler performs.
